title: MongoDB WiredTiger Storage Engine
learnerQuestion: What should I understand about WiredTiger beyond the name of MongoDB's default storage engine?
coreClaim: WiredTiger turns MongoDB operations into page, cache, version, journal, checkpoint, and recovery work.
mechanism: MongoDB server semantics are translated into WiredTiger B-tree tables, update chains, cache pages, eviction, logging, and checkpoints.
example: Multi-document insert and operational revenue aggregation.
counterpoint: WiredTiger internals explain mechanisms, but MongoDB server semantics and deployment context still determine user-visible behavior.
practicalTakeaway: Reason about storage symptoms through concrete engine mechanisms.

title: What You Should Be Able To Reason About
learnerQuestion: What practical decisions should this deck help me make?
coreClaim: Engine literacy helps diagnose cache pressure, dirty eviction, checkpoint work, query page traffic, version retention, and durability behavior.
mechanism: Learning goals map MongoDB operations to WiredTiger structures and operational counters.
example: Use `serverStatus().wiredTiger`, profiler output, and `explain()` together.
counterpoint: Engine metrics are not sufficient without workload shape and OS/cloud context.
practicalTakeaway: Use the deck as a diagnostic and design checklist.

title: We Will Trace Two Concrete Operations
learnerQuestion: Which workloads will make the internals concrete?
coreClaim: A batch insert and an aggregation read expose most important WiredTiger mechanisms from write amplification to page fetches and spills.
mechanism: The anchors exercise collection/index B-trees, transactions, write concern, optimizer/planner choices, cache, and spill paths.
example: Order-event insert batch and operational revenue aggregation.
counterpoint: Other workloads add sharding, replication topology, or workload-specific access patterns.
practicalTakeaway: Track one write path and one read path throughout the deck.

title: MongoDB Operations Cross Server, Engine, And OS Boundaries
learnerQuestion: Where does MongoDB end and WiredTiger begin?
coreClaim: MongoDB owns command/query semantics while WiredTiger owns storage mechanics under those semantics.
mechanism: Command path -> query/write execution -> storage cursor -> WiredTiger cache/B-trees -> journal/checkpoint -> filesystem cache/data files.
example: A write can be acknowledged by MongoDB while also creating dirty pages and journal/checkpoint work below.
counterpoint: The OS filesystem cache and cloud storage layer can dominate latency even when engine behavior is correct.
practicalTakeaway: Diagnose across layers instead of assigning every symptom to the storage engine.

title: WiredTiger Is Not Just The File Format
learnerQuestion: What does WiredTiger actually do at runtime?
coreClaim: WiredTiger is the runtime system for B-trees, pages, cache, MVCC, eviction, reconciliation, checkpoints, logging, and recovery.
mechanism: Storage tables maintain pages and update chains in memory, then reconcile and persist durable images through checkpoints and logs.
example: A dirty leaf page must be reconciled before eviction or checkpoint persistence.
counterpoint: MongoDB's server layer still decides query plans, write concern, aggregation behavior, and replication semantics.
practicalTakeaway: Treat engine tuning as runtime-system tuning, not file tuning.

title: MongoDB Owns Semantics; WiredTiger Owns Storage Mechanics
learnerQuestion: Which layer should I blame or inspect for a symptom?
coreClaim: User-visible semantics such as write concern, transactions, aggregation stages, and indexes are MongoDB concerns implemented through lower-level WiredTiger operations.
mechanism: MongoDB uses WiredTiger sessions/cursors/tables to execute semantic operations.
example: `$sort` is a MongoDB aggregation stage; WiredTiger experiences the resulting cursor reads and page fetches.
counterpoint: A server-level semantic choice can still create storage-engine pressure.
practicalTakeaway: Map symptoms to both semantic operation and storage mechanism.

title: A MongoDB Collection Maps To Several WiredTiger Tables
objective: Explain collection and index storage mapping.
learnerQuestion: Why does one logical collection write create multiple physical writes?
coreClaim: A collection and each index are separate storage structures, so writes multiply across B-trees.
mechanism: Collection data and secondary indexes are separate WiredTiger tables with independent page and cache effects.
example: Inserting one order event writes the collection and each secondary index.
counterpoint: The exact catalog/storage naming is internal, but the write amplification principle is stable.
practicalTakeaway: Count indexes as write, cache, checkpoint, and recovery cost.

title: Pages Are The Unit You Keep Paying For
learnerQuestion: What does an index or collection lookup touch inside WiredTiger?
coreClaim: B-tree root, internal, and leaf pages are the units of traversal, caching, dirtying, eviction, and checkpointing.
mechanism: Search traverses internal pages to leaf pages; writes dirty leaf pages and may alter page structure.
example: A range scan over an index reads adjacent leaf pages and may fetch collection pages.
counterpoint: MongoDB reports documents and keys examined, not every page-level internal detail.
practicalTakeaway: Think in pages when diagnosing cache and I/O behavior.

title: Why B-Trees Fit MongoDB's Access Patterns
learnerQuestion: Why are B-trees central to MongoDB storage and indexes?
coreClaim: B-trees support point lookups, ordered traversal, range scans, and prefix locality required by common MongoDB access patterns.
mechanism: Ordered keys guide traversal and make adjacent-key scans efficient when indexes match query and sort shape.
example: An index on `{ customerId: 1, createdAt: -1 }` can narrow by customer and walk recent orders.
counterpoint: A B-tree only helps when index key order matches predicates and sort requirements.
practicalTakeaway: Design indexes around traversal shape, not only field presence.

title: An Update Chain Is The Engine's Local Version History
learnerQuestion: How can readers see old values while writers create new ones?
coreClaim: WiredTiger update chains preserve versions so visibility checks can choose the right value for a transaction or snapshot.
mechanism: Updates attach versioned entries to keys; transaction and timestamp visibility decide which version is readable.
example: A long-running aggregation may need an older version while newer writes continue.
counterpoint: Version retention is useful for consistency but can increase cache/history pressure.
practicalTakeaway: Old snapshots can have storage costs even when they are read-only.

title: MongoDB Uses Logical Time To Coordinate Visibility And Stability
learnerQuestion: How does WiredTiger know which versions are stable or discardable?
coreClaim: Stable, oldest, and pinned timestamps coordinate visibility, rollback safety, and history cleanup.
mechanism: Stable timestamp marks work that cannot be rolled back; oldest timestamp bounds future reads; pinned timestamp is constrained by active reads.
example: A stale active read can pin history and delay cleanup.
counterpoint: Timestamp behavior is coordinated by MongoDB server logic; internal details vary by release.
practicalTakeaway: Connect long reads and transactions to version-retention symptoms.

title: The History Store Is Not A Query Feature; It Is MVCC Infrastructure
learnerQuestion: Why can old versions consume engine resources?
coreClaim: The history store supports MVCC visibility and cleanup, not application querying.
mechanism: Older versions can be retained outside the primary update chain when needed for timestamped visibility.
example: Old snapshots or transactions can retain history that eviction/checkpoint must account for.
counterpoint: The deck abstracts implementation details; use metrics and release-specific docs for exact behavior.
practicalTakeaway: Treat history-store activity as a version-retention diagnostic clue.

title: There Are Two Caches In The Path, With Different Contents
objective: Separate WiredTiger cache from filesystem cache.
learnerQuestion: Why does MongoDB use memory outside the WiredTiger cache?
coreClaim: WiredTiger cache and filesystem cache hold different representations and serve different roles.
mechanism: WiredTiger cache holds engine pages; filesystem cache holds OS-cached file blocks, often closer to compressed on-disk data.
example: Collection data is uncompressed in WiredTiger cache but compressed on disk and in filesystem cache representation.
counterpoint: A larger WiredTiger cache can reduce filesystem cache headroom.
practicalTakeaway: Do not diagnose memory by WiredTiger cache size alone.

title: Eviction Is The Engine's Backpressure System
learnerQuestion: What happens when the WiredTiger cache fills?
coreClaim: Eviction frees cache by removing pages, but dirty or versioned pages make that work more expensive.
mechanism: Eviction selects pages, checks visibility, reconciles dirty pages if needed, and removes pages from cache.
example: Foreground application threads may participate in eviction when pressure is high.
counterpoint: Eviction symptoms can be caused by page traffic, dirty-byte pressure, or old-version retention.
practicalTakeaway: Read eviction metrics as pressure signals, not as the root cause by themselves.

title: Dirty Eviction Is Where Logical Versions Become Page Images
learnerQuestion: Why are dirty pages harder to evict?
coreClaim: Dirty eviction must reconcile in-memory updates into a page image that can be safely written or tracked.
mechanism: Reconciliation evaluates updates, visibility, page layout, and durable state before producing a new disk-ready representation.
example: An insert-heavy workload with many secondary indexes creates dirty pages across several B-trees.
counterpoint: Clean page eviction is cheaper because it can discard cache state without writing a new image.
practicalTakeaway: Dirty-byte growth points to write/reconciliation/checkpoint pressure.

title: A Checkpoint Is A Consistent Durable Base Image
learnerQuestion: What does a checkpoint do that the journal does not?
coreClaim: A checkpoint records a consistent durable view of data files that recovery can start from.
mechanism: Checkpoint walks modified state and makes durable metadata point to a consistent set of page images.
example: After a crash, WiredTiger can start from the last checkpoint and replay logs after it.
counterpoint: A committed write may exist after the last checkpoint and still depend on log replay.
practicalTakeaway: Separate checkpoint durability from individual write acknowledgement.

title: The Write-Ahead Log Protects Changes Between Checkpoints
learnerQuestion: How are writes protected before the next checkpoint?
coreClaim: The WiredTiger log/journal records changes so recovery can replay work after the last checkpoint.
mechanism: Write-ahead log records operations before data-file checkpoint state fully reflects them.
example: If MongoDB exits between checkpoints, journal replay recovers data modified since the last checkpoint.
counterpoint: Write concern determines when clients are told a write is acknowledged, which is layered above engine logging.
practicalTakeaway: Use journaling, checkpoint, and write concern as separate diagnostic terms.

title: Commit, Journal, And Checkpoint Are Different Moments
objective: Put durability events on one timeline.
learnerQuestion: Which event actually makes a write durable or visible?
coreClaim: Engine commit, journal persistence, client acknowledgement, checkpoint, and recovery are separate events.
mechanism: Transaction state, log records, checkpoint metadata, replication, and write concern interact across layers.
example: A write can be committed in memory, logged for recovery, acknowledged by write concern, and checkpointed later.
counterpoint: Exact timing depends on configuration, deployment, and write concern.
practicalTakeaway: Ask which durability boundary a symptom refers to.

title: The Workload: Inserting Order Events
learnerQuestion: What concrete write workload will expose storage costs?
coreClaim: A batch of order events exercises collection writes, index writes, transaction visibility, write concern, and recovery paths.
mechanism: `insertMany()` turns a logical batch into repeated document and index mutations.
example: Order events with customer, timestamp, status, and SKU indexes.
counterpoint: Real workloads add validation, shard routing, retryable writes, and replication behavior.
practicalTakeaway: Use a concrete batch to reason about write amplification.

title: One Batch Turns Into Many Engine-Level Changes
learnerQuestion: What happens below one `insertMany()` call?
coreClaim: Each document and index entry creates storage-engine mutations even when the client sees one batch call.
mechanism: Validate -> allocate record -> insert into collection B-tree -> insert into each index B-tree -> mark transaction visibility -> log/checkpoint later.
example: A 1,000-document batch with four indexes creates thousands of B-tree entry changes.
counterpoint: Bulk execution can reduce command overhead and oplog shape, but not eliminate per-entry storage work.
practicalTakeaway: Estimate storage work as documents times touched indexes.

title: ordered Changes Failure Behavior, Not Storage Fundamentals
learnerQuestion: Does unordered insertion make the storage work disappear?
coreClaim: `ordered` controls whether the batch stops after an error; it does not remove collection and index mutation costs.
mechanism: Ordered inserts stop after most write errors; unordered inserts continue remaining operations.
example: Duplicate-key error in an unordered batch still leaves successful earlier/later documents and their index writes.
counterpoint: Driver and retry behavior can affect client-visible handling; engine-level writes still need consistency.
practicalTakeaway: Choose ordered/unordered for failure semantics, not as a storage tuning shortcut.

title: MongoDB's Write Unit Has To Keep Collection And Indexes Consistent
learnerQuestion: Why can't MongoDB update collection and index data independently?
coreClaim: A write must preserve consistency between the collection record and all affected index entries.
mechanism: MongoDB coordinates the collection and index mutations inside the write unit and transaction machinery.
example: If an insert succeeds, its unique and non-unique index entries must match the collection state.
counterpoint: Application-level multi-document atomicity requires transactions and additional overhead.
practicalTakeaway: Index consistency is part of write latency and failure behavior.

title: Each Secondary Index Adds A Second Write Workload
learnerQuestion: Why do extra indexes slow writes and increase cache pressure?
coreClaim: Each secondary index adds another B-tree mutation stream with its own pages, dirty bytes, and checkpoint work.
mechanism: Index key derivation and index B-tree insert/update dirty pages independently of collection pages.
example: Indexes on customer, SKU, status, and createdAt add separate write paths.
counterpoint: Indexes may still be worth the cost when they prevent expensive reads or blocking sorts.
practicalTakeaway: Treat every index as both a read optimization and a write/storage cost.

title: Uniqueness Turns Inserts Into Reads Plus Writes
learnerQuestion: Why are unique indexes more expensive during insert?
coreClaim: Unique indexes require conflict detection in addition to index mutation.
mechanism: MongoDB must verify that a candidate key does not violate uniqueness before committing the insert.
example: Unique order number index checks for an existing key before allowing the new entry.
counterpoint: The extra cost buys a strong correctness guarantee that application code should not reimplement casually.
practicalTakeaway: Expect unique constraints to add read pressure to write paths.

title: Transactions Widen The Lifetime Of Versions And Resources
learnerQuestion: Why can transactions affect storage-engine pressure?
coreClaim: Transactions can retain versions, locks/resources, and visibility state longer than simple single-document writes.
mechanism: Transaction snapshots and commit/abort decisions interact with update chains and timestamps.
example: A transaction that updates several order documents can hold versions until commit or abort.
counterpoint: Transactions are correct for some workflows, but docs warn they are not a substitute for effective schema design.
practicalTakeaway: Use transactions deliberately and monitor their version-retention footprint.

title: Client Acknowledgement Layers Above Engine Commit
learnerQuestion: Why can a write seem slow after engine work is done?
coreClaim: Write concern adds acknowledgement requirements above local storage-engine mutation.
mechanism: Client acknowledgement can depend on local durability and replica acknowledgement according to write concern.
example: `w: majority` waits for a different boundary than a local in-memory mutation.
counterpoint: Lower write concern can reduce acknowledgement latency but changes durability/consistency risk.
practicalTakeaway: Separate local engine latency from replication/acknowledgement latency.

title: Recovery Reconstructs The Boundary Between Stable And Unstable Work
learnerQuestion: What happens after MongoDB restarts following a crash?
coreClaim: Recovery starts from checkpoint state, replays logs, and resolves stable versus unstable work.
mechanism: Last checkpoint plus log replay plus timestamp/transaction stability determines recovered state.
example: Writes after the last checkpoint may be replayed from the journal.
counterpoint: Long replay or rollback-to-stable work can make restart time workload-dependent.
practicalTakeaway: Explain restart time through checkpoint, journal, and stable timestamp boundaries.

title: The Workload: Operational Revenue Aggregation
learnerQuestion: What read workload will expose query and storage costs?
coreClaim: An aggregation over revenue data stresses predicate pushdown, index order, fetches, blocking stages, and spill behavior.
mechanism: Pipeline optimization and planning determine the storage cursor work WiredTiger must perform.
example: Filter recent paid orders, sort, group by account or region, and compute revenue metrics.
counterpoint: Aggregation behavior depends on pipeline shape, indexes, collection statistics, and server version.
practicalTakeaway: Analyze aggregation as server execution plus storage access.

title: The Storage Engine Sees Cursor Work, Not A Pipeline
learnerQuestion: Does WiredTiger know about `$match`, `$sort`, or `$group`?
coreClaim: WiredTiger serves cursor reads and page requests; MongoDB owns the pipeline semantics.
mechanism: Optimizer/planner/executor converts pipeline stages into index scans, collection scans, fetches, and temporary work.
example: `$match` may become an index scan; `$group` may become server memory work over cursor results.
counterpoint: Storage symptoms still reflect the plan chosen by the server.
practicalTakeaway: Fix the plan when the engine is only doing what it was asked to do.

title: Aggregation Optimization Decides What Can Reach Indexes Early
learnerQuestion: How can pipeline order change storage work?
coreClaim: The aggregation optimizer can move or split stages so filters and limits reach indexes earlier when dependencies allow.
mechanism: Optimization rewrites pipeline stages such as `$match`, projections, sort/limit coalescence, and eligible index use.
example: Moving `$match` before projection can reduce documents entering later stages.
counterpoint: Optimizations are subject to change between releases and cannot overcome every dependency.
practicalTakeaway: Use `explain()` to see the optimized shape, not just the written pipeline.

title: The Planner Turns Predicates Into B-Tree Traversal Choices
learnerQuestion: How does a query predicate become page traffic?
coreClaim: Planner choices determine whether WiredTiger traverses a narrow index range, wide index range, or collection scan.
mechanism: Index bounds, sort requirements, fetches, and covered projections determine cursor access.
example: A selective prefix index narrows leaf-page traversal; a missing prefix can scan far more pages.
counterpoint: Planner behavior is server-level and may change by version and statistics.
practicalTakeaway: Read index bounds and keys/docs examined as storage-work predictors.

title: A Covered Plan Can Avoid Collection Page Fetches
learnerQuestion: Why can an index-only plan be much cheaper?
coreClaim: Covered plans can satisfy a query from index keys without fetching collection pages.
mechanism: If predicates, sort, and projected fields are available in an index, server execution can avoid collection document fetches.
example: A dashboard query returning accountId, status, and createdAt from a matching compound index.
counterpoint: Covered plans require projection discipline and index fields; they may increase write/index storage cost.
practicalTakeaway: Use covering to trade index storage for fewer collection page reads.

title: $sort And $group Are Memory-Shaping Stages
learnerQuestion: Why do sort and group stages create memory and disk pressure?
coreClaim: `$sort` and `$group` can require blocking memory and may spill when stage limits or conditions require disk use.
mechanism: Server execution buffers sorted or grouped state before producing downstream results.
example: Revenue grouped by account over a wide time window can hold many group keys.
counterpoint: Indexes and optimizer rewrites can reduce or eliminate blocking work in some shapes.
practicalTakeaway: Treat blocking stages as memory design decisions.

title: Aggregation Spill Is Not The Same As WiredTiger Eviction
learnerQuestion: If an aggregation spills to disk, is that WiredTiger eviction?
coreClaim: Aggregation spill is server temporary-file work, while WiredTiger eviction is cache page management.
mechanism: Blocking aggregation stages may write temporary files; WiredTiger eviction reconciles and removes cache pages.
example: `usedDisk` in profiler points to aggregation spill, while `wiredTiger.cache` counters point to engine eviction.
counterpoint: Both can contribute to disk pressure and must be correlated with OS metrics.
practicalTakeaway: Use the right metric family for the right disk-pressure mechanism.

title: Reads Pay For Old Versions When Old Snapshots Are Still Valid
learnerQuestion: How can reads create storage-engine pressure?
coreClaim: Long-running snapshots can force old versions to remain visible and delay cleanup.
mechanism: Pinned timestamps and visibility checks retain update history until old readers no longer need it.
example: A long aggregation over old snapshot state while writes continue.
counterpoint: Short reads that use current versions may not create meaningful version-retention pressure.
practicalTakeaway: Correlate long reads with history and cache pressure.

title: Document-Level Concurrency Lives Below Intent Locks
learnerQuestion: How can MongoDB allow concurrent writes without collection-level serialization?
coreClaim: MongoDB uses multi-granularity intent locks while WiredTiger provides document-level concurrency below collection locks.
mechanism: Server locks coordinate global/database/collection intent; WiredTiger handles finer-grained conflict detection and concurrency.
example: Two writes to different documents in the same collection can proceed concurrently unless they conflict on storage state.
counterpoint: Hot documents, unique indexes, transactions, and long-running operations can still create contention.
practicalTakeaway: Diagnose contention by distinguishing lock waits from write conflicts and hot data.

title: Start By Mapping The Symptom To A Mechanism
learnerQuestion: How should I start debugging a storage-engine symptom?
coreClaim: Effective diagnosis starts by mapping symptoms to page traffic, dirty bytes, version retention, checkpoint/log work, query spills, or platform pressure.
mechanism: Symptom -> candidate mechanism -> profiler/explain/serverStatus/OS evidence -> targeted fix.
example: High dirty bytes points to write/checkpoint pressure, not necessarily bad reads.
counterpoint: Many incidents involve multiple mechanisms at once.
practicalTakeaway: Use a mechanism-first diagnostic order.

title: serverStatus().wiredTiger Is The First Engine Readout
learnerQuestion: Which MongoDB output tells me what WiredTiger is experiencing?
coreClaim: `serverStatus().wiredTiger` exposes cache, eviction, checkpoint, transaction, block-manager, and related engine counters.
mechanism: Rate and correlate counters over the same interval as workload symptoms.
example: Compare application-thread eviction, dirty bytes, pages read into cache, checkpoint time, and transaction counters.
counterpoint: Raw cumulative counters are less useful than rates and correlations.
practicalTakeaway: Graph rates, not just snapshots.

title: explain() Tells You How Much Storage Work The Plan Requested
learnerQuestion: How do I see whether a query asked for too much storage work?
coreClaim: `explain()` exposes plan shape, indexes, scans, fetches, and execution stats that predict storage work.
mechanism: Read winning plan, index bounds, keys examined, docs examined, stages, and execution stats.
example: High docs examined relative to returned rows indicates excess collection page fetches.
counterpoint: Explain output is a server-planner view; pair it with engine and OS metrics.
practicalTakeaway: Fix plan shape before tuning engine knobs.

title: Use Multiple Instruments Because No Single One Owns The Whole Path
learnerQuestion: Why do I need profiler, explain, serverStatus, and OS metrics?
coreClaim: MongoDB performance symptoms cross semantic, engine, and platform layers that no single metric fully explains.
mechanism: Profiler identifies operation shape; explain identifies plan; serverStatus identifies engine pressure; OS/cloud metrics identify resource limits.
example: Aggregation spill plus storage latency plus checkpoint pressure can overlap.
counterpoint: More metrics can distract if they are not tied to a concrete symptom window.
practicalTakeaway: Correlate metrics over the same time interval.

title: Schema Design Changes Page And Index Locality
learnerQuestion: How does document design affect WiredTiger work?
coreClaim: Schema shape changes document size, update locality, index fan-out, page churn, and version-retention behavior.
mechanism: Embedded arrays, growing documents, hot fields, and index key patterns alter pages touched and update chains created.
example: A hot status field in many secondary indexes dirties multiple index pages per update.
counterpoint: Denormalization can reduce read page traffic even if it increases write size.
practicalTakeaway: Model schema as a storage-access pattern.

title: Index Design Is A Storage Budget, Not Only A Query Feature
learnerQuestion: How should I decide whether an index is worth it?
coreClaim: Indexes trade write/cache/checkpoint cost for narrower reads, fewer fetches, and less blocking work.
mechanism: Each index adds B-tree maintenance while potentially reducing scanned keys/documents and avoiding sorts.
example: A compound index can cover a dashboard query but adds insert and update cost.
counterpoint: Unused or redundant indexes are pure storage and write overhead.
practicalTakeaway: Evaluate indexes with both read and write budgets.

title: Batching Changes Overhead Shape, But Not Atomic Work Per Document
learnerQuestion: How much does batching reduce write cost?
coreClaim: Batching reduces command overhead and can improve throughput, but each document and index entry still creates storage work.
mechanism: `insertMany()` packages many inserts, while collection and index B-tree mutations still occur per affected entry.
example: A larger batch may improve throughput but also create larger dirty-byte bursts.
counterpoint: Batch size can harm latency, replication lag, or checkpoint pressure if pushed too far.
practicalTakeaway: Tune batch size against throughput, latency, dirty bytes, and replication.

title: Aggregation Design Either Narrows Early Or Pays Late
learnerQuestion: What is the simplest rule for storage-friendly aggregation?
coreClaim: Aggregation should reduce candidate documents early and use indexes before late blocking stages expand memory or page traffic.
mechanism: Early `$match`, compatible sort/index order, projection reduction, and covered plans reduce downstream work.
example: Filter by time/customer before grouping revenue across accounts.
counterpoint: Some business questions require wide scans or blocking stages; then capacity and spill planning matter.
practicalTakeaway: Narrow early or budget for late-stage cost.

title: Be Cautious With Knobs That Hide Design Problems
learnerQuestion: Which fixes are likely to mask the real issue?
coreClaim: Cache, compression, compaction, batch, and write concern knobs can hide poor operation shape if applied before diagnosis.
mechanism: Knobs change resource allocation or acknowledgement boundaries but may not reduce pages touched, dirty bytes, or versions retained.
example: Increasing cache may delay eviction while an unbounded scan still touches too many pages.
counterpoint: Knobs are valid after the workload mechanism is understood.
practicalTakeaway: Tune after mechanism diagnosis.

title: Common Symptoms And First Questions
learnerQuestion: What should I ask first when I see a common WiredTiger symptom?
coreClaim: Each symptom points to a short list of candidate mechanisms that should guide the first diagnostic questions.
mechanism: Map cache dirty bytes, app-thread eviction, disk growth, spills, write conflicts, and restart delay to likely mechanisms.
example: Aggregation spill asks for stage memory and index-order review, not cache-size tuning first.
counterpoint: Symptoms can overlap; confirm with metrics before fixing.
practicalTakeaway: Turn symptoms into targeted questions.

title: A Practical Diagnostic Order
learnerQuestion: What order should I follow when debugging?
coreClaim: Start with operation shape, then storage pressure, then platform pressure over the same time window.
mechanism: Profiler/explain -> `serverStatus().wiredTiger` rates -> OS/cloud/disk/replication metrics.
example: For a slow aggregation, inspect plan and spill before changing WiredTiger cache size.
counterpoint: Emergency mitigation may require parallel operational action while root cause is being isolated.
practicalTakeaway: Use a consistent diagnostic order to avoid random tuning.

title: The Engine Mental Model
learnerQuestion: What should I remember after the details?
coreClaim: Writes create collection/index mutation and durability work; reads request cursor/page/version work; operations surface page, dirty, and version pressure.
mechanism: Insert path, aggregation path, and diagnostic path all reduce to B-trees, cache, versions, and durability boundaries.
example: Order inserts and revenue aggregation are two expressions of the same engine primitives.
counterpoint: Sharding, replication topology, and cloud storage add additional layers not fully covered here.
practicalTakeaway: Keep the page/dirty/version model in mind.

title: How To Think In WiredTiger Terms
learnerQuestion: How should I apply this in design and operations?
coreClaim: WiredTiger-aware design treats indexes, snapshots, missing indexes, durability, and knobs as storage mechanisms with tradeoffs.
mechanism: Every index adds B-tree cost; every old snapshot can retain versions; every missing index can create page traffic; every durability setting moves acknowledgement boundaries.
example: Before changing cache, check query shape, index budget, and transaction lifetime.
counterpoint: Engine-aware thinking should support product requirements, not override correctness or durability needs.
practicalTakeaway: Connect design choices to storage mechanisms before tuning.

title: Follow-up Reading
learnerQuestion: Where can I verify or go deeper?
coreClaim: MongoDB manual pages define user-visible behavior; WiredTiger architecture guides explain mechanism-level internals with release caveats.
mechanism: References are grouped by storage behavior, architecture, writes/durability, and aggregation/query execution.
example: Use MongoDB docs for production behavior and WiredTiger architecture docs for B-tree, transaction, eviction, checkpoint, and logging internals.
counterpoint: WiredTiger architecture docs explicitly may not match every release exactly.
practicalTakeaway: Verify version-sensitive claims against the current MongoDB manual and release-specific behavior.
